I feel very old now. I remember having to set up a GeoCities site when I was in highschool. If I recall correctly, it was the final project for a HTML programming class.

I think in the case of the search engines is that they turned off all their customers by trying to turn them into web portals. So every time you wanted to search for something you had to download pages and pages of crap.

The services providers simply became redundant when people started to connect to the internet directly. I think that some of them tried to rebrand themselves as ISPs but that never panned out.

You only have to look back at things like Anglefire and GeoCites (and Myspace for that matter but that was later on) to understand why they went broke. My eyes the goggles do nothing.
If I recall they mixed up ads with genuine search results because they wanted more money. Google on the other hand separated ads, and made their engine to run as fast as possible.
Google also did some really strange tricks with their servers (such as building them 'sideways' to save space) that led to them saving a LOT of money, so they could afford to have less ads (etc.).
http://neocities.org/ is an attempt to recreate Geocities.

I kinda predate all that. My first experience with the Internet was using both Archie and Veronica to access what was then the Internet, which, by the way, was all text. There was one browser called Mosaic, but Archie and Veronica were the early almost-search engines. You had to know what you were looking for because it was all mostly FTP directories at that time. The Internet was almost a language unto itself.

Oddly enough, Geocities isn't dead it's just Japan only.

Just like the English geocities, if you hunt around you can find some interesting stuff.
